title: Khaybar
year: 7 AH — 628 CE, from the end of Muharram to early Rabi'ul-Awwal
teaser: Two months after a treaty that looked like surrender, the army marched north against eight fortresses.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: The northern oasis that never stopped working
layers.content:
Khaybar lay sixty to eighty miles north of Madinah — the distance is given as a range, not a figure — a spacious and strongly fortified territory studded with castles and farms, rich enough in soil and orchards that its dates were famous across the Hijaz. Today it is a village with a reputation for unhealthy air.

With Quraysh neutralised by the treaty, two members of the old alliance against Madinah remained: the Jews of the north and the Bedouin of Najd. Khaybar came first, and the reasons are set out plainly by al-Mubarakpuri. It had always remained a hotbed of intrigue and conspiracy, a source of military provocation and a centre of instigation. Bound to the Confederates by an ancient alliance, its leadership had pushed Banu Qurayzah into treachery during the siege of Madinah, kept up contact with Ghatafan and the hostile Arabs, and devised a plot on the Prophet's life. Envoys had been sent repeatedly for a peaceful settlement. All of them came back with nothing.

Ibn Ishaq records the timing: he came back from al-Hudaybiyah, stayed in Madinah through Dhul-Hijjah and part of Muharram, and left at the end of Muharram. Siba' bin 'Arfatah al-Ghifari was left in charge of the city. In the same weeks a man from Daws accepted Islam whose name would end up attached to more hadith than almost any other — Abu Hurayrah.

Only those willing to fight in the cause of Allah were invited to come. The printed figures for the force do not agree and this chapter will not choose between them; what The Sealed Nectar states without ambiguity is that two hundred of them were cavalry, and that every man there had asked to be there.

Abdullah bin Ubai got word out ahead of the army, warning Khaybar to resist because the Muslims were fewer and worse equipped. Khaybar sent Kinanah bin Abul-Huqaiq and Haudhah bin Qais to Ghatafan for troops, offering half of one year's fruit harvest as the price.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Road to Khaybar
layers.subtitle: A camel-driver's verses and a morning nobody expected
layers.content:
He marched by the 'Isr mountain and halted in a valley called ar-Raji', camping a day and a night short of Ghatafan so that they could not reinforce the oasis. At a junction where several roads all led to Khaybar, he refused three of them for what their names meant and took the fourth for the better omen in its name.

They travelled at night. Salamah bin al-Akwa' relates that a man asked his brother 'Amir to chant verses to urge the camels on. 'Amir sang: O Allah, if You had not guided us, we would have neither been rightly guided, nor practised charity, nor offered prayers. We wish to lay down our lives for You, so forgive us our lapses and keep us firm when we meet them. The Prophet ﷺ asked who the camel-driver was. They told him. He said, Allah will show mercy to him. A man answered at once: martyrdom is reserved for him, O Messenger of Allah — would that you had let us keep him a while. They had learned that he never asked mercy for a Companion by name except to mark him out for death. Al-Bukhari and Muslim both carry it.

At a place called as-Sahba' he prayed Asr and asked for whatever provisions the men had. What came was not enough for them; he took it in his hand, it increased, and they all ate their fill. Then they rinsed their mouths and he prayed Maghrib without renewing ablution, and Isha the same way.

Coming up above the oasis and looking down into it he said: Halt. Then: O Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and what they cover, Lord of the seven earths and what they contain, Lord of the devils and what they mislead — we ask You for the good of this town and its people, and seek refuge with You from its evil and theirs. Proceed, in the Name of Allah.

They camped that night without the Jews knowing they were there. In the morning the farmers came out with axes, spades and cords, driving their cattle, and saw an army. Muhammad has come with his force, they shouted.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Salamah bin al-Akwa' — the march to Khaybar and the verses of his brother 'Amir
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Banner and the Forts
layers.subtitle: Sixteen days of walls and one sentence about guidance
layers.content:
He answered: Allah is Great, Khaybar is ruined. When we descend among a people, it dawns a bad day for those who were warned.

Eight forts mattered: five in the north, in an-Natah and ash-Shaq, and three behind them in the section called al-Katibah. Al-Hubab bin al-Mundhir, who had corrected the choice of ground at Badr, did it again and had the camp moved for mobility.

The night before, he said he would give the banner in the morning to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love. He called for 'Ali bin Abi Talib, whose eyes were inflamed, prayed over them until the illness went, and handed him the banner. 'Ali pledged to fight them until they accepted Islam. The Prophet ﷺ answered: go until you are among them, then invite them to Islam and tell them what is due to Allah from them. By Allah, if one man is guided through you, that is better for you than the best of camels.

Na'im fell first. Marhab, its commander, called 'Amir bin al-Akwa' out to single combat; 'Amir's own sword recoiled and cut his knee, and he died of it. 'Ali then met Marhab and killed him, and az-Zubair killed his brother Yasir. As-Sa'b was stormed after three days, its stores falling to men so hungry they had been cooking domestic donkey; he ordered the meat thrown out and the pots washed.

Az-Zubair fort lay beyond cavalry and infantry both, until an informer told him of an underground water source; it was cut, they came out, and it fell. Ubai took three days, and Abu Dujanah of the red headband broke into it. An-Nizar stood highest, held the women and children, and answered with arrows and stones until catapults cracked its walls.

Al-Katibah endured fourteen days and asked for terms as the catapults were readied. Whether it fell by force or by treaty is disputed: Ibn Ishaq says al-Qamus was taken by force, al-Waqidi that all three came by negotiation. Reports on the Muslim dead differ between sixteen and eighteen. The Jewish dead are given as ninety-three.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the banner given to 'Ali bin Abi Talib and the instruction to invite before fighting
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: A promise cashed, and a request refused in advance
layers.content:
The verses that govern Khaybar came down before it, in the surah revealed about the treaty. Commentators on the Qur'an read the capture of the oasis as the divine promise implied in «وَعَدَكُمُ اللَّهُ مَغَانِمَ كَثِيرَةً تَأْخُذُونَهَا فَعَجَّلَ لَكُمْ هَٰذِهِ» — 'Allah has promised you abundant spoils that you will capture, and He has hastened for you this.' (48:20) The promise was given to men riding home from a journey on which they had gained nothing, had been turned back from the Ka'bah, and had signed terms that felt like a humiliation. Two months later the wealthiest oasis in the north was in their hands.

The second verse settled a question before it was asked. Those who had stayed behind when al-Hudaybiyah looked like a death sentence would come forward when the next march looked like profit: «سَيَقُولُ الْمُخَلَّفُونَ إِذَا انطَلَقْتُمْ إِلَى مَغَانِمَ لِتَأْخُذُوهَا ذَرُونَا نَتَّبِعْكُمْ» — 'Those who lagged behind will say, when you set forth to take the spoils: Allow us to follow you.' They wish to change the Word of Allah. Say: you shall not follow us; thus Allah has said beforehand. (48:15) The answer was on record before the request existed.

That principle then shaped the division of the land. Half of Khaybar went to those who had been present at al-Hudaybiyah, whether or not they fought at Khaybar. The share followed the pledge given under the tree, not the risk taken at the walls.

Two rulings also come out of this campaign rather than any sermon about it. Domestic donkey meat was forbidden in the middle of a famine, with the pots already on the fire. And the prayer at as-Sahba' — mouths rinsed after eating, Maghrib prayed without renewing ablution, and Isha likewise — is preserved in al-Bukhari as a point of law, taken from a hungry army on a night march.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the prohibition of domestic donkey meat at Khaybar, and the prayer at as-Sahba'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: Full stomachs, a marriage, and a taste he never lost
layers.content:
The terms were that they leave Khaybar and the land around it and hand over their gold and silver, the guarantee void if anything was concealed. Something was. A leather bag of jewels belonging to Huyai bin Akhtab, carried out when Banu Nadir were exiled, had been hidden by Kinanah bin ar-Rabi', who denied it until it was found. He was killed for it, and Abul-Huqaiq's two sons with him, for breaking the covenant.

Then the Jews of Khaybar asked to stay. They did not want to leave the soil and the orchards, and offered to work them for half the produce. He agreed. The land was divided in two: one half held as a food reserve against calamity and for the delegations now arriving, the other half as thirty-six shares, eighteen of them to the people of al-Hudaybiyah.

What that meant is easiest to hear from those who ate it. Ibn Umar: we never ate our fill until we conquered Khaybar. Aishah: now we can eat our fill of dates. Back in Madinah the Emigrants could at last return to the Helpers every gift they had been given.

Safiyah bint Huyai, whose father and husband had both been killed, was among the captives. He invited her to Islam, freed her, and married her; the wedding meal on the road home was dates, fat and barley. Fadak sued for peace without a fight, Wadi al-Qura surrendered after about two days, Taima' offered tribute unasked, and he reached Madinah in late Safar or early Rabi'ul-Awwal.

One thing did not end. Zainab bint al-Harith, a woman of Khaybar, sent him a roasted sheep she had poisoned; he took a mouthful, disliked it, and spat it out. She admitted it: if he were a king she would be rid of him, and if he were a Prophet he would be told. He let it pass, until Bishr bin al-Bara' died of the same meat.

Carry this. Years later, dying in Aishah's room, he said: I still feel the painful effect of the food I tasted at Khaybar. I feel as if death is approaching. The greatest material victory of his life arrived with a poison in it, and he knew, and he went on.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — Ibn Umar and Aishah on the plenty after Khaybar; Sahih al-Bukhari — the marriage to Safiyah, and his words about the food of Khaybar in his final illness
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: The night before the assault, the Prophet ﷺ said he would give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom they love. Who received it?

options.text: Al-Hubab bin al-Mundhir, who had chosen the camp
Abu Dujanah, the man with the red headband
'Ali bin Abi Talib, whose inflamed eyes were healed first
Az-Zubair bin al-Awwam

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Preparing to Fight and the Good News of Victory
quiz.scholar_reflection: Every man in the camp spent the night hoping it meant him. The one who got it was the one who could not see well enough to hold it until the Prophet ﷺ prayed over his eyes.

quiz.prompt: 'Ali pledged to fight the people of Khaybar until they accepted Islam. What did the Prophet ﷺ tell him to do?

options.text: To take the fort first and speak to them afterwards
To reach them, invite them to Islam, and tell them what was due to Allah from them
To wait for the catapults before advancing
To demand the surrender of Kinanah bin Abul-Huqaiq

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the banner at Khaybar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He added the measure to go with it: if one man is guided through you, that is better for you than the best of camels. The camels of Khaybar were about to be counted in the thousands.

quiz.prompt: How did 'Amir bin al-Akwa' die in his single combat with Marhab, the commander of the fort of Na'im?

options.text: Marhab struck him down with a spear
He was hit by an arrow from the wall above
His own sword recoiled and wounded his knee, and he died of the wound
He fell from the wall while scaling it

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Actual Operation Begins
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was the camel-driver whose verses had carried the army through the night, and the man for whom mercy had already been asked. The Prophet ﷺ put two fingers together and said he had a double reward.

quiz.prompt: The surrender terms at al-Katibah spared lives on condition that nothing was concealed. What was found hidden?

options.text: Weapons buried beneath the date orchards
A leather bag of jewels and money that had belonged to Huyai bin Akhtab
Letters from Abdullah bin Ubai in Madinah
Fighters from Ghatafan sheltering inside the fort

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Negotiations, and the breach of the covenant at Khaybar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Huyai had carried it out of Madinah when Banu Nadir were exiled. Kinanah bin ar-Rabi' denied the bag existed until it was produced. His wife, Safiyah, later became the Prophet's wife.

quiz.prompt: Did the three forts of al-Katibah — al-Qamus, al-Watih and as-Sulalim — fall by force or by negotiation?

options.text: By force, and every historian agrees on it
The sources disagree — Ibn Ishaq says al-Qamus was taken by force, al-Waqidi says all three came over by treaty
They were abandoned before the Muslims arrived
They were destroyed by the catapults

quiz.citation: Ibn Ishaq and al-Waqidi, the disagreement recorded in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Conquest of the Second Section of Khaibar
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar names the disagreement rather than resolving it. What both accounts agree on is that the forts asked for terms while the catapults were being brought up.

quiz.prompt: At the moment the banner was handed over, with eight forts ahead, he said that guiding one man was better than the best of camels. Why say that then?

options.text: Because a man about to fight is the one most likely to forget it
It sets the price of the whole campaign so nobody mistakes the spoils for the point
It was for 'Ali personally, who had just pledged to fight until they submitted
It reads well but the forts still had to be stormed, and they were

quiz.slider_label: Take the fort — Guide one man
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the instruction given with the banner
quiz.scholar_reflection: Note that 'Ali's pledge was the ordinary soldier's instinct and it was corrected on the spot. Invite first. The fighting was permitted; it was not the objective.

quiz.prompt: The men who stayed home when al-Hudaybiyah looked like death asked to join the march that looked like profit, and were refused by a verse revealed in advance. How do you read the refusal?

options.text: A cost missed is a cost missed; there is no back payment for it
It is harsh — men should be allowed to correct themselves
It protected the meaning of the pledge for the ones who kept it
The refusal was about their motive, and the motive had not changed

quiz.slider_label: Let them earn it now — The moment has passed
quiz.citation: Quran 48:15 — al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, Headed to Khaibar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Half the land went to the people of al-Hudaybiyah whether or not they fought at Khaybar. Presence at the frightening thing was the qualification; presence at the profitable thing was not.

quiz.prompt: The defeated people of Khaybar asked to stay on the land they had just lost and farm it for half the produce. He agreed. What do you make of that?

options.text: Practical — nobody else knew how to work those orchards
It leaves a defeated enemy sitting on the ground, which is a risk
The war was over the plotting, not the people, so it ended when that did
Letting a beaten man keep his work is a kind of mercy that costs nothing

quiz.slider_label: Clear the land — Keep them on it
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Distribution of Spoils
quiz.scholar_reflection: The agreed terms had been that they leave. They asked to stay, and The Sealed Nectar says he was kind enough to accept their request. The men executed at Khaybar were executed for the concealed bag, not for being there.

quiz.prompt: Zainab bint al-Harith confessed to poisoning him, reasoning that a king would die and a Prophet would be told. He let it pass, and ordered her killed only after Bishr bin al-Bara' died of the same meat. Where do you sit?

options.text: The attempt alone deserved the penalty; the delay was mercy, not justice
He forgave what was done to him and could not forgive what killed another man
Punishment tracking actual harm rather than intent is the sounder rule
Her own reasoning convicted her, and the outcome merely proved it

quiz.slider_label: Punish the attempt — Wait for the harm
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Poisoned Sheep, with the basis of the report in Sahih al-Bukhari
quiz.scholar_reflection: The distinction in the account is exact. Her attempt on his own life he ignored. The death of a Companion he did not.

quiz.prompt: Khaybar was the campaign that ended hunger in Madinah, and the campaign that put a poison in him he still felt on his deathbed. What do you do with a victory that carries its own wound?

options.text: Take it — every real gain in this world is paid for in something
It reframes the spoils: dates in the store, poison in the body
He carried it for four years without saying so, which is the actual lesson
It makes me suspicious of calling any outcome a clean success

quiz.slider_label: The wound outweighs it — The victory holds
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari — his words in his final illness, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: The sentence is recorded in his last days: I still feel the painful effect of the food I tasted at Khaybar. Between the mouthful and the sentence lie the opening of Makkah, Tabuk, and the whole of Arabia.
